sources.text:
Kennedy Center votes to restore Trump’s name
A May court ruling ordered the center to remove the president’s name from the building
What happened
President Donald Trump’s handpicked Kennedy Center board voted Thursday to add his name back to the building’s facade and follow through with his plan to close most of the center for two years of renovations. This apparent “attempt to find a creative workaround” to the federal law governing the Kennedy Center also “aggressively” tests U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper’s May ruling that blocked the center’s closure and ordered Trump’s name removed, The New York Times said.
Who said what
The board decided the center’s facade would now read “The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump,” and its grounds would be renamed “President Donald J. Trump Plaza,” according to Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), the ex-officio board member who successfully sued to get Trump’s name excised. The new decisions are a “transparent effort to circumvent the court’s ruling,” Beatty said in a statement.
The Kennedy Center has become an “unlikely — and highly visible — metaphor for presidential power” in Trump’s second term, The Associated Press said. His name was removed in June, but a “massive tarp” has shielded the court-ordered void from public view. Board member and longtime Trump ally Paolo Zampolli told the Times his goal was to reinscribe Trump’s name “as big as it can get.”

The board of trustees for the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., voted on Thursday to place President Donald Trump’s name on the outside of the building, testing a previous court order that blocked the renaming of the institution after the president.
The change is a loophole of sorts. While the vote doesn’t attempt to rename the building after Trump, it does place a new inscription on the building in an attempt to honor him.
During the first month of his return to office, Trump fired all of the board of trustees and replaced them with his own handpicked loyalists. The board eventually voted to rename the center by placing his name ahead of Kennedy’s, and for a time, the building was known as “The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts.”
But a federal judge ruled earlier this year that the move violated congressional dictates requiring that the center be named after former President John F. Kennedy and no one else.
By law, Congress had made “crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board’s unilateral say-so,” U.S. District Judge Casey Cooper determined.
Trump’s name was eventually removed from the center’s exterior. But on August 13, the board voted to continue renovations of the building and to place a new inscription on its exterior that reads “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”
The board also voted to rename the center’s grounds to the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”
Cooper had stipulated in his ruling that the renaming of the building and other planned renovations had to be put on hold so the board could consider how the changes would affect the Kennedy Center’s performance schedule and its congressionally mandated programming. The board determined in its vote this week that renovations could move forward while a smaller stage remained open to performances, hoping to navigate around Cooper’s stipulations.
The board must submit its changes for approval to the federal court by August 18.
On Thursday night, CNN’s Kaitlan Collins noted that Trump’s obsession with remaking national fixtures in his image wasn’t limited to the Kennedy Center.
“The president’s focus has not just been on the Kennedy Center in terms of his broader push to remake Washington. It’s also his penchant for branding everything in his name,” Collins opined. “That includes the gold coins, the Trump passports, the National Park passes, the Palm Beach airport — I’m not done — the banner at the Justice Department, the new class of battleships. There are many things, not just in Washington, but all across the nation now bearing the Trump name.”
When Trump’s name was removed from the building earlier this summer, some artists celebrated the restoration of the venue’s intended name to honor Kennedy, not the current president.
Trump’s name being removed from the building in June “really does mean something,” said Mallory Miller, former assistant manager of dance at the center, who was fired last August. “This is just the first step in rebuilding the trust that has been lost.”

sources.news_title: Kennedy Center’s Trump name dispute heads toward another court clash
sources.text:
The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to add a tribute to Trump to the building’s facade and rename the surrounding grounds “President Donald J. Trump Plaza,” according to Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex officio member of the board.
The move is particularly striking because a federal judge ruled just months ago that the Kennedy Center could not be formally renamed for Trump without an act of Congress.
What the Kennedy Center plans to put on the building
Rather than replacing the Kennedy Center name entirely, the board voted to add the words “Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump” to the facade.
The site itself would carry the separate Trump Plaza designation.
The decision appears designed to recognize Trump while preserving the center’s existing formal name — a distinction that could become central to the legal battle now taking shape.
Beatty, who has already sued over the administration’s changes at the Kennedy Center, said the board’s latest decision attempts to get around the court’s earlier ruling. The Kennedy Center did not immediately comment, while the White House praised Trump’s role in reshaping the institution.
Why Trump’s name was removed in the first place
The dispute dates back to December, when the Trump-dominated board voted to put his name on the Kennedy Center.
That decision was challenged in federal court. In May, US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that the board did not have the authority to officially rename the center because Congress had established it as a memorial to President John F. Kennedy.
The court declared the previous renaming effort legally invalid and ordered the removal of Trump’s name from official references and signage.
Workers eventually removed the lettering from the building in June after appeals courts declined to keep the Trump signage in place while the legal fight continued.
Trump’s board now wants a two-year shutdown
The naming dispute is unfolding alongside another controversial decision.
The board also voted to close the Kennedy Center for roughly two years for renovations, according to Beatty. The plan has already been the subject of litigation, with questions raised over how the closure would affect the institution’s cultural mission and finances.
A court had previously scrutinized the proposed shutdown and demanded more information about its necessity and potential consequences.
The board’s latest vote means the future of the Kennedy Center is now tied to two major questions: how far its Trump-aligned leadership can go in changing the institution, and whether those decisions can withstand continued court challenges.
A new legal fight could be coming
The latest move does not erase the earlier ruling that Congress controls the center’s formal name.
That leaves a potentially important distinction between renaming the institution and adding language to its facade or giving the surrounding grounds a new designation.
For Trump and his allies, the changes are part of an effort to overhaul what they view as an outdated and financially troubled institution. Critics, including Beatty, see them as an attempt to sidestep federal law and turn a national memorial into a political project.
The Kennedy Center board is now pushing ahead despite the court history, meaning the next chapter may be decided not by a vote inside the building, but by another battle in federal court.
(With Reuters inputs)

The Kennedy Center’s board of trustees on Thursday voted to put President Donald Trump’s name on the institution’s facade in Washington, D.C., testing the limits of a judge’s order on the matter.
The board voted to add the inscription “Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump” below the Kennedy Center sign, according to Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH), who sits on the board. The physical site outside the building is also set to be renamed “the President Donald J. Trump Plaza,” after Beatty said Thursday’s vote sought to “circumvent” U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper’s ruling blocking Trump’s name from being added to the Kennedy Center’s official title.

Beatty is the individual who brought a lawsuit challenging the center’s name change last December to “The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts.”
Cooper, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama, sided with Beatty in late May, ruling that the Kennedy Center’s board exceeded its authority when it unanimously voted to add Trump’s name to the center in December. The judge said congressional approval is required to change the institution’s name, meaning the center’s signage bearing Trump’s name must be removed. The judge also blocked the theater’s planned two-year closure for extensive renovations.
At the time, the Kennedy Center said it was complying with the court’s order “while evaluating all legal options to preserve this revitalization and recognize President Trump’s leadership.”
Beatty slammed the board after it appeared to seek to work around the ruling from Thursday’s vote and suggested it would revive the legal battle in court.

The board of trustees for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to temporarily close the facility’s main building for a major renovation project, and to affix President Donald Trump’s name to the exterior facade. The decision comes months after a federal judge struck down a prior attempt to rename the cultural institution and halted a scheduled full shutdown of the venue.
Under the newly approved plan, the arts complex will undergo a $250 million overhaul, which includes structural repairs, fresh marble flooring, and $12 million dedicated to acoustical enhancements. To facilitate the work, the trustees chose “to close the Kennedy Center’s main building, while keeping a newer addition to the campus, known as the Reach, open for limited programming and to operate as an active memorial to John F Kennedy”. The main campus is scheduled to remain closed for two years, with a targeted reopening set for the summer of 2028.
In addition to the closure, the board—composed largely of presidential appointees—voted to add an inscription beneath the venue’s existing exterior signage that reads, “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump.” The move directly tests a May ruling by U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who determined that earlier efforts to modify the official name violated federal statute because only Congress holds the authority to alter the memorial’s designation. Cooper had previously blocked the center’s planned closure after finding the initial board vote was “ill-informed and seemingly preordained”.
Opponents of the decision quickly signaled plans for further legal action. Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, who sits on the board and previously sued to stop the changes, condemned the latest vote as “a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed.” Her attorneys added, “Today’s vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts,” noting that “The court already ruled against the board when it bowed to Trump’s demands. Now, the defendants must answer for their actions—again—in court.”
White House officials defended the board’s decision, praising the scope of the planned upgrades. Executive spokesperson Liz Huston stated, “Under President Trump’s bold leadership, the Kennedy Center is on its way to becoming the finest cultural institution anywhere in the world.” The board’s latest determinations remain subject to review by Judge Cooper, who will assess whether trustees conducted sufficient due diligence before submitting their updated plans next week.

sources.news_title: Kennedy Center board decides to inscribe Trump’s name on building
sources.text:
Kennedy Center board decides to inscribe Trump’s name on building
The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to inscribe President Donald Trump’s name on the building beneath the main signage, according to two people with direct knowledge of the proceedings, aggressively testing a federal judge’s order.
According to the resolution approved by the Trump-allied board, the inscription underneath the institution’s name would read: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”
ADVERTISING
The board’s decision, which directs officials to act by “all legal means,” came shortly after it voted to move forward with Trump’s plan to shutter the building for renovations.
The president’s name was added to the building last year, but the judge ordered the letters taken down, finding that only Congress had the authority to change the institution’s name.
The center removed Trump’s name in June but is appealing the ruling.
The move appeared to be a creative workaround to a provision in the federal law governing the Kennedy Center that says “no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas.”
Both decisions will be subject to the scrutiny of the judge who found that the board had been “derelict” in considering the closure plan before its original vote.
The board voted Thursday to close the Kennedy Center’s main building, while keeping a newer addition to the campus, known as the Reach, open for limited programming and to operate as an active memorial to President John F. Kennedy.
Before the meeting, the board was presented with a 163-page plan for a $250 million “renewal” project that includes structural repair work, new marble floors, $11.8 million in “acoustical improvements” and a plan to temporarily move the famous 3,000-pound bronze bust of Kennedy to another building on campus.
The approved resolution notes that the decision to close was made based on an “independent and objective analysis” of possible options by an outside consulting firm, which determined that keeping the main building open during renovations would be significantly more costly.
Judge Christopher R. Cooper of U.S. District Court in Washington will soon review the decision to consider whether the trustees, in his view, performed enough due diligence before the vote.
The Kennedy Center has until next week to share its plan with Cooper.

sources.news_title: Trump’s Name Could Return to Kennedy Center
sources.text:
The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to put President Donald Trump’s name back on the building — just two months after a federal judge ordered it removed.
The latest move follows an earlier attempt to rename the institution. Last year, the Trump-allied board voted to change the center’s name to the Trump-Kennedy Center, and Trump’s name was quickly added to the building’s marble facade.
U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper ruled in May that the change violated federal law, which established the center as a memorial to President John F. Kennedy. Cooper found that only Congress has the authority to change the center’s name and ordered Trump’s name removed from the building and official materials. The center complied in June but is appealing the ruling.
Now the board is taking a different approach.
Rather than formally renaming the center, it approved an inscription beneath the Kennedy Center’s main signage that would read: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”
The move appears to be an attempt to return Trump’s name to the building without technically changing the institution’s official name — and could test the limits of Cooper’s order as well as federal law governing memorials at the center.
The board resolution directs officials to honor Trump by “all legal means” for what it describes as his role in bringing the center back “from the brink of disaster.” Other possibilities reportedly include naming the grounds the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”
Center Will Close for Renovations
The board also voted Thursday to move forward with Trump’s plan to close the Kennedy Center’s main building for approximately two years while extensive renovations are completed.
A newer part of the campus, known as the Reach, would remain open for limited programming and serve as the active memorial to Kennedy during construction.
Plans presented to the board outline about $250 million in work, including structural repairs, new marble flooring, theater improvements, updated equipment, redesigned interior spaces, new restrooms and $11.8 million in acoustical improvements. The target reopening is summer 2028.
Trump has described the Kennedy Center as “tired, broken and dilapidated” and has argued that closing it entirely would allow renovations to be completed more quickly and safely.
But the closure has become entangled with another problem facing the institution: declining programming, ticket sales and participation by artists following Trump’s takeover of the center.
Trump replaced much of the Kennedy Center board in 2025 with allies, who then elected him chairman. Since then, prominent artists have canceled appearances or severed ties with the institution, employees have departed and ticket sales have declined.
Broadway touring productions have gone elsewhere for the coming season, while the National Symphony Orchestra has yet to announce a season that would normally begin in September.
That turmoil has fueled questions about whether the two-year closure is solely about construction.
Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who holds an ex officio seat on the Kennedy Center board, raised that issue in her lawsuit challenging the closure. She argues the shutdown could help mask a financial downturn caused in part by declining ticket sales and artists refusing to perform at the center.
The board maintains its decision was based on an independent analysis concluding that keeping the building open during phased renovations would be substantially more expensive and raise safety concerns.
Cooper previously blocked the closure after finding that the board’s original decision was based on a “one-sided presentation of information” and failed to adequately consider the center’s legal obligation to both maintain and operate the national performing arts venue.
The judge will now review whether the board conducted sufficient due diligence before Thursday’s new vote.
That review could determine not only whether the Kennedy Center can close for two years, but whether Trump’s name can once again appear prominently on a building Congress designated as a memorial to John F. Kennedy.

The board voted to recognize President Donald Trump’s work to improve the location, and then to shut it down for two years for the repairs to be made without endangering the public.
Largely similar actions had been adopted by the board earlier, but Christopher Cooper, a judge owing his job to Barack Obama, ordered Trump’s name be barred from the building, and that the board had to run it for events even during reconstruction.

The board found a simple workaround, announcing that the inscription would be altered to state that it is the Kennedy Center, “restored and renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”
Further the plaza where the building sites now will be Trump plaza.
A report at the Hill said the board earlier had added Trump’s name to the title of the center, but that was reversed on Cooper’s orders.
Board members also decided that the two-year closure was the best way to handle major repairs.
Trump had fired members of the center board last year and named his own appointees.
The objections to the board’s earlier plans were raised by Rep. Joyce Beatty, a Democrat from Oregon, who sued.
Beatty, on hearing the new decision, claimed it was an attempt to “circumvent” the court, and “flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed.”
The center also has appealed the judge’s demands, so his ruling may eventually be inapplicable anyway.

Board members, many of whom are Trump allies, voted to add "Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump" to the formal name of the centre on Thursday, according to Democratic Congresswoman Joyce Beatty, who sits on the board.

The board also voted on Thursday to proceed with a two-year closure for proposed renovations, which was earlier blocked by a federal judge.

The judge ordered that the name be removed, and so it was taken down last month despite a last‑minute attempt by the Trump administration to pause the order.
An appeals court declined to intervene immediately, allowing the removal to proceed pending further arguments.
The Trump administration had argued that changing the centre's name could create confusion if the decision were later overturned.

Trump announced the addition of his name to the institution, among other rebranding measures across the nation's capital, last year.
In February 2025, he replaced several trustees on the centre's board and appointed himself as a trustee before being voted in as the arts centre's chairman.

sources.text:
Kennedy Center board votes to inscribe Trump’s name on building
The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted today to inscribe President Donald Trump’s name on the building beneath the main signage, according to two people with direct knowledge of the proceedings, aggressively testing a federal judge’s order.
According to the resolution approved by the Trump-allied board, the inscription underneath the institution’s name would read: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.” The board’s decision, which directs officials to act by “all legal means,” came shortly after it voted to move forward with Trump’s plan to shutter the building for renovations.
The president’s name was added to the building last year, but the judge ordered the letters taken down, finding that only Congress had the authority to change the institution’s name. The center removed Trump’s name in June but is appealing the ruling.
The move appeared to attempt to find a creative workaround to a provision in the federal law governing the Kennedy Center that says “no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas.”
In today’s resolution, the board directed officials to honor Trump for bringing the center back “from the brink of disaster,” presenting a series of possibilities that included naming the center’s grounds the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”
“It is hereby resolved,” the measure said, “that the center desires to recognize and honor President Trump’s existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the center by all legal means.”

Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Both decisions will be subject to the scrutiny of the judge who, in response to a lawsuit from a Democratic lawmaker, found that the board had been “derelict” in considering the closure plan before approving it originally. Trump announced in February that the center would close for two years, with the objective of transforming what he called a “tired, broken and dilapidated” institution.
The board voted today to close the Kennedy Center’s main building, while keeping a newer addition to the campus, known as the Reach, open for limited programming and to operate as an active memorial to President John F. Kennedy.
Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio and an ex officio member of the center’s board who sued the center, said in a statement that the resolutions were part of a “transparent effort to circumvent the court’s ruling.” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, another Democratic ex officio member, called the vote to close a “rubber stamp” on the original directive from the president.
In a phone interview after the votes, Paolo Zampolli, a former modeling agent and a longtime Trump ally who sits on the board, said the trustees acted out of a desire to make the Kennedy Center more of a sought-after sightseeing destination. His goal for the inscription of Trump’s name is to make it “as big as it can get,” he said.
Before the meeting, the board was presented with a 163-page plan for a $250 million “renewal” project that includes structural repair work, new marble floors, $11.8 million in “acoustical improvements” and a plan to temporarily move the famous 3,000-pound bronze bust of Kennedy to another building on campus. The judge had said in his order that the board had a legal obligation to maintain the facility as a memorial to Kennedy.
The approved resolution noted that the decision to close was made based on an “independent and objective analysis” of possible options by an outside consulting firm, which determined that keeping the main building open during renovations would be significantly more costly. It notes that the board was “fully committed” to continue arts and educational programming during the closure and maintain the “historic and architecturally significant nature” of the building.
Trump, the board’s chair, called into the meeting, which was held remotely, and criticized those opposed to his closure plan, according to the people with direct knowledge of the proceedings.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who was tapped by the president to help oversee the Kennedy Center, strongly endorsed the plan, the people said, at one point crediting the president, a developer by trade, with an ability to keep construction projects on schedule and on budget.
After Trump announced the closure plan this year, the board quickly agreed. But Judge Christopher Cooper of U.S. District Court in Washington temporarily blocked the closure, ruling that the original vote had been “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” In his order in May, the judge wrote that the center’s trustees had a legal obligation to seriously consider the potential consequences of shuttering Washington’s preeminent performing arts venue.
Trump lashed out at the judge following his decision and said it would be “dangerous” to keep the center open. Center officials later assured the judge that they were following his order and further scrutinizing the decision, culminating in the meeting today.
Cooper will soon review the board’s resolution to consider whether the trustees, in his view, performed enough due diligence before the vote.
“The board will be expected to prepare itself with sufficient information to make a considered, independent decision,” the judge wrote in the May order, “taking account of its obligation to both maintain and operate a premiere arts venue and its solemn duty to memorialize a fallen president.”
For weeks, the future of the Kennedy Center has been in limbo, with a largely bare performance calendar.
Broadway touring shows, typically a major source of ticket revenue, have gone elsewhere. The National Symphony Orchestra, the center’s resident ensemble, has yet to announce a season that typically opens in late September. And employees at the center, which already executed rounds of layoffs, remain unsure about their futures.
The resolution approved by the board noted that during the closure, the orchestra would perform at outside venues, and the Kennedy Center Honors, the institution’s marquee event, would also be held off-site.
Before the meeting, trustees were provided with a comparison of two scenarios for renovations by an outside consultant. Both the consultant and the construction management firm, JLL, raised safety and cost concerns that they said would arise from keeping the building open during a phased renovation.
The proposal by JLL said the project would address chronic leaks, replace outdated equipment and redesign parts of the interior. Changes would include new furniture, a new coffee shop, electronic ticketing kiosks and $7 million in public restroom renovations. The target for reopening would be summer of 2028.
It was unclear immediately after the meeting, which was not public, whether the center intends to pursue the exact construction plan laid out in the report.
Over the past year and a half, the Kennedy Center has struggled with an exodus of audience members, employees and artists unwilling to be involved with what they now view as a political arm of the White House. The backlash was particularly strong late last year, when the board voted to change the institution’s name to the Trump-Kennedy Center. New letters were added to the building’s marble facade the next day.
Cooper ruled that changing the center’s name required approval from Congress, which dedicated the institution to Kennedy in 1964, shortly after he was assassinated. Before the center removed “Trump” from the building, it also installed a towering matrix of scaffolding, covered in tarps, that obscures much of the current signage.
Many of the board members are staunch Trump allies, such as Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff; Dan Scavino, a Trump adviser; and Allison Lutnick, a former lawyer who is married to Lutnick.
In an interview in June at a Kennedy Center event to honor comedian Bill Maher, Howard Lutnick said Trump asked him to get involved to make sure the board’s processes were in line with the court’s expectations.
“He asked me to help him make sure everything is organized,” Lutnick said, “so that when judges consider what the board is doing, that it’s done perfectly.”
Matt Floca, the center’s executive director, has argued that a full closure would be the most efficient and responsible way to execute sorely needed renovations using the $257 million allotted by Congress last year. In a report for the board, Delta Consulting Group, which was hired to compare different scenarios for renovations, said that if the center pursued a phased construction process over four years, the congressional appropriation would cover less than half of the estimated costs.
Outside arts administrators have suggested the financial realities for cultural organizations are far different from what the board is projecting, saying institutions typically do anything possible to avoid closure so they do not lose ticket revenue and donors. Beatty’s lawsuit questioned the true reasoning for the closure plans, arguing that it may be an effort to mask a financial downturn stemming from the president’s takeover.
The Kennedy Center has until next week to share its plan with Cooper.

His efforts to put his stamp on the Kennedy Center arts complex in Washington -- blocked earlier this year by a federal judge -- moved ahead once again on Thursday.

The New York Times and The Washington Post, citing unnamed sources with knowledge of the proceedings, said the inscription would go directly below the main signage.

The Kennedy Center did not immediately reply to AFP's request for comment on the board's proceedings.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, former reality TV star Trump has aggressively imprinted his personal brand on institutions, eschewing political tradition.
The Kennedy Center's board initially voted in December to rename the venue as "The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts."
The Republican president's name was quickly added to the facade in large letters above that of Kennedy, spurring the cancellation of shows and plunging ticket sales for remaining events.

Kennedy Center Board Approves Trump Plaza, Plans to Restore Trump’s Name to Building
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Kennedy Center board voted Thursday to designate the grounds surrounding the famed performing arts venue as “President Donald J. Trump Plaza” and to restore Trump’s name to the building’s exterior, following a federal judge’s order that it be removed.
The measures were approved by Trump-aligned board members during a meeting that stretched beyond two hours. The vote came over objections from Democrats, including Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, who criticized Trump’s proposed renovation and rebranding of the aging Washington landmark.
Trump, who serves as chair of the Kennedy Center board, joined part of the session remotely and defended his plan to invest $250 million in upgrades to the cultural institution, which first opened in 1971. The renovation project is expected to shutter the main building for roughly two years.
Under the board’s new approach, Trump’s name would be placed below the existing lettering inside the center’s expansive main hall, with signage reading: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”
The board had previously voted in December to rename the venue the “Trump Kennedy Center,” but that move was blocked by U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who ruled that adding the sitting president’s name required approval from Congress.
Democratic lawmakers quickly condemned the board’s latest decision.
“This morning’s decision to close the Center and the surprise agenda item to put Donald Trump’s name back on the building was more of the same,” Beatty said in a statement. “This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed.”
Paolo Zampolli, a Trump appointee to the board, pushed back sharply against the criticism, calling for the president’s name to be displayed prominently and dismissing objections to the temporary shutdown as ignoring the scale of repairs and modernization work the Kennedy Center needs.
“I call on everyone who is complaining about what we’re doing to go walk the building,” Zampolli told The Post. “To all of the haters, we’re not closing the center. We’re closing the main building. We’re still going to use the $300 million structure called the Reach to do shows.”
The center’s staff did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.
“Under President Trump’s bold leadership, the Kennedy Center is on its way to becoming the finest cultural institution anywhere in the world,” said White House spokeswoman Liz Huston.

But opponents argue the distinction between renaming the Kennedy Center and memorializing Trump on its facade may not survive scrutiny under the same federal law that produced Cooper’s earlier ruling.
Norm Eisen, the former White House ethics lawyer who represents Beatty alongside Nathaniel Zelinsky, sharply criticized Thursday’s vote. “A federal judge already rejected the board’s unlawful attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, and told Donald Trump’s handpicked board that its last closure vote was ill-informed and preordained,” Eisen said.
“Today’s vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts.”
Eisen added in another statement that “the court already ruled against the board when it bowed to Trump’s demands. Now, the defendants must answer for their actions — again — in court.”
Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democrat who sits on the Kennedy Center board through her congressional position, also condemned the vote.
“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” said Beatty, who brought the initial lawsuit challenging Trump's name on the Kennedy Center. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”
What Is The 'Loophole?'
The board is no longer attempting to call the institution the “Trump-Kennedy Center.”
Instead, the resolution would leave the Kennedy Center’s official name intact while adding a separate inscription crediting Trump for its restoration and renovation.
That distinction could be central to the legal battle.
Judge Cooper wrote in May that the Kennedy Center’s governing statute “makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy” and that Congress, rather than the board, has the authority to change that name. His order required Trump’s name to be removed from the Center's physical and digital branding.
The board's latest resolution, however, goes beyond the wording on the facade. It also proposes honoring Trump through other physical spaces, including a possible President Donald J. Trump Plaza.
Democracy Defenders Action, which represents Beatty in the litigation, argues that the statute expressly restricts additional memorials or plaques in the Center's public areas.
Lawyer Harry Litman warned that the Kennedy Center Board, who he described as being "composed of Trump acolytes" was "inviting a showdown with Judge Cooper," with the latest proposal.
"They vote to add to the building, inscribed, 'restored and renovated by Pres Donald J. Trump' below JFK. See you in court!" he warned.
Closure Vote Could Create a Second Legal Fight
The name isn't the only issue headed back before Judge Cooper. The board also voted to close the Kennedy Center's main building for two years while a roughly $250 million renovation takes place. The newer Reach building would remain open for limited programming.
The judge had previously blocked the closure, saying the board's initial decision was based on a “one-sided presentation of information” and that the trustees had neglected their broader statutory obligations to the institution. He characterized the original decision as “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.”
The judge did not say the Kennedy Center could never close for construction. Rather, he left open the possibility that the board could reach that conclusion after conducting a genuinely independent assessment of its competing obligations. Reuters reported after the May ruling that Judge Cooper specifically said the board could close the Center if it reached that decision anew after independently balancing those obligations.
The board says it has done precisely that: it considered alternatives and received outside analysis supporting a full closure.
But Beatty's legal team is likely to ask whether the process was sufficiently independent — particularly because Trump announced the two-year closure months before Thursday's supposedly fresh decision.
Trump announced plans to close the center for a two-year renovation project in February, following a wave of cancellations by musicians and performers after he added his name to the building and ousted previous leadership.
“This important decision, based on input from many Highly Respected Experts, will take a tired, broken, and dilapidated Center, one that has been in bad condition, both financially and structurally for many years, and turn it into a World Class Bastion of Arts, Music, and Entertainment,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Statute May Complicate the Board's Workaround
There is another potential problem for the board's strategy.
Democracy Defenders Action argues that the Kennedy Center's governing statute expressly prohibits additional “memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials” in public areas, subject to narrow exceptions. The organization says that provision could independently undermine Thursday's proposed inscription and the proposed Trump Plaza.
That means the board may have created a legal argument that is actually broader than the original naming dispute.
If the court concludes that the proposed inscription is effectively a new memorial to Trump, the board could face the question of whether it has violated not merely the court's prior order but the underlying statute itself.
Who Is On The Kennedy Center Board?
Trump has reshaped the Kennedy Center's board since taking control of the institution in 2025, replacing or removing trustees and installing a group of allies and administration officials.
The board includes :
- Trump himself as chairman,
- White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles,
- adviser Dan Scavino,
- Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's wife Allison Lutnick,
- and other prominent Trump supporters, alongside members who serve by virtue of their government positions.
- Rep. Beatty holds an ex officio seat on the board and has become one of the most prominent critics of Trump's efforts to reshape the institution. Court records in Beatty's lawsuit list dozens of trustees as defendants, including Trump, Wiles, Scavino, Lutnick and other political allies.
The board's composition has become central to the legal dispute because Beatty has argued that trustees who are politically aligned with Trump have failed to exercise the independent judgment required of them in making decisions about the Kennedy Center's name, operations and future.
Will the Kennedy Center Close Again?
The Kennedy Center board voted Thursday to close the main building for roughly two years while a $250 million renovation is carried out, reversing the effect of a federal judge's earlier order that blocked the original closure plan.
The board says the shutdown is necessary to carry out major structural and mechanical work safely and efficiently. A renovation plan presented to trustees considered both a full closure and a phased approach, with outside consultants concluding that keeping the building operating during construction would be substantially more expensive. The plan calls for the main building to reopen in summer 2028, while the Reach, a newer part of the Kennedy Center campus, would remain open for limited programming.
But the decision still faces scrutiny from U.S. District Judge Cooper, who previously blocked the closure after finding that the board's original decision-making process was “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” The question now is not simply whether the Center needs repairs, but whether the board genuinely reconsidered the consequences of closing the nation's premier performing-arts memorial after the judge ordered it to do so.
Will Trump's Name Be Added to the Kennedy Center?
Judge Cooper ruled in May that the board did not have the authority to rename the Kennedy Center after Trump and ordered references to his name removed. The Center complied in June, removing Trump's name from its facade and official materials.
The board's latest vote would add his name to the building as part of a statement that said, “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” beneath the Kennedy Center's existing name. The board also directed officials to pursue “all legal means” to recognize Trump for what it describes as his contributions to the Center's survival.
Once again, the move will now be subject to Judge Cooper's scrutiny.
Which Parts of the Kennedy Center Will Be Renamed?
The board has not voted to formally rename the Kennedy Center itself as the Trump-Kennedy Center. Instead, Thursday's resolution calls for Trump's name to be added to the building as a restoration dedication and proposes naming the grounds “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”
That distinction is important because Judge Cooper previously ruled that Congress — not the Kennedy Center board — has the authority to change the institution's statutory name. The board's new strategy appears to be to preserve the official John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts name while creating separate spaces and inscriptions honoring Trump.
What Is the Kennedy Center Chuck Redd Lawsuit?
The Chuck Redd case is a separate lawsuit that illustrates how the Kennedy Center's attempt to add Trump's name affected artists as well as the institution's governance.
Redd, a jazz musician who had performed an annual Christmas Eve “Jazz Jam” at the Kennedy Center for years, canceled his 2025 performance after Trump's name was added to the building. The Kennedy Center subsequently sued Redd for breach of contract and sought damages, after then-Kennedy Center president Richard Grenell had threatened him with a $1 million claim. Redd's lawyers argued that he had never signed a contract requiring him to perform and that the lawsuit was an attempt to punish him for protesting the renaming.
A D.C. Superior Court judge dismissed the Kennedy Center's lawsuit in June under the District's Anti-SLAPP law, which is designed to protect speech and other activity on matters of public interest. The court found that the Center had failed to establish a valid breach-of-contract claim.
The legal fallout continued this week. On August 11, the judge ordered the Kennedy Center to pay Redd $252,479.70 in legal fees and costs after his successful defense. The Center has indicated that it intends to appeal.
The Redd case is separate from Beatty's federal lawsuit over the Kennedy Center's name and closure, but it has become another legal consequence of the Trump-led transformation of the institution — and another example of the disputes that followed the original decision to put Trump's name on the building.
What Happens Next
For now, Thursday's vote does not mean Trump's name can legally be placed back on the Kennedy Center.
The Kennedy Center has until next week to share its plan with Judge Cooper, who is expected to assess whether the board's new approach complies with his earlier ruling and the Kennedy Center's governing statute.
“The board will be expected to prepare itself with sufficient information to make a considered, independent decision,” the judge wrote in his May order. He added that it must take into account "its obligation to both maintain and operate a premiere arts venue and its solemn duty to memorialize a fallen president.”

sources.text:
Apparently, taking Donald Trump’s name off the Kennedy Center wasn’t the end of the story. It was just a design problem.
President Trump’s handpicked board of the Kennedy Center has voted again to close the performing arts institution for renovations — and this time, the board also found a new way to put Trump’s name on the building without technically renaming it.
According to two people briefed on the decision, the board voted Thursday to add an inscription beneath the Kennedy Center’s existing sign reading: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”
Because apparently the building itself wasn’t enough.
The board also voted to keep the REACH, a separate part of the Kennedy Center complex, open during the renovations. The smaller facility would continue hosting more limited programming while the main building undergoes a planned two-year closure, CNN reports.
The move comes after months of legal and political chaos surrounding one of Washington’s most prominent cultural institutions.
Trump made reshaping the Kennedy Center a priority during his second term. Earlier this year, he announced plans to shut the center down for renovations, arguing that the facility was in poor condition.
Then came the naming controversy.
In December, the board voted to rename the institution the “Trump Kennedy Center.”
There was just one problem. Congress had already named it the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
And a federal judge wasn’t particularly impressed with the board’s attempt to rewrite that.
In May, U.S. District Judge Casey Cooper blocked the planned two-year closure, ruling that the board needed to consider maintaining some programming during the renovations so the center could continue carrying out its congressionally mandated functions.
Cooper also ruled that the board had violated the law by adding Trump’s name to the performing arts venue.
The law establishing the center, Cooper wrote, makes clear that it is to be named for President Kennedy and cannot simply be given another formal name or memorial at the board’s discretion.
So in June, Trump’s name was removed from the Kennedy Center’s facade following the court order.
Problem solved?
Not quite. The center’s name is still covered by large tarps.
And now Trump’s name is apparently coming back — just underneath the sign instead of as part of the institution’s official name.
One source briefed on Thursday’s vote argued that the inscription isn’t technically an attempt to rename the Kennedy Center.
That’s one way to look at it.
Another source described the inscription as a “permanent reminder” of his undermining of the institution.
Either way, the message is difficult to miss.
Trump’s name may not officially be part of the Kennedy Center’s name, but the board appears determined to make sure visitors see it anyway.
And the timing couldn’t be more awkward for an institution already struggling to get back on its feet.
The Kennedy Center has dealt with falling ticket sales, artists pulling out of performances, political controversy and a depleted staff.
The original shutdown plan had already generated intense scrutiny.
Now the institution is preparing for another lengthy closure while trying to maintain at least some programming at the REACH.
And hanging over all of it is the increasingly bizarre question of how many different ways Trump’s name can appear on a building Congress explicitly named after John F. Kennedy.
The court said the Kennedy Center can’t be formally renamed by the board.
So the board appears to have found another option: Don’t rename the building. Just put Trump’s name underneath it.
Technically different.
Politically, not exactly subtle.

sources.text:
The battle over the Kennedy Center’s future escalated Thursday as President Donald Trump’s allies on the board took new steps to commemorate him with physical changes to the iconic performing arts institution that could defy a federal court order.
During an hourslong meeting that was conducted virtually, the board voted to add Trump’s name to the building’s facade so it would read “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump.” The plaza in front of the building would be named after Trump and most of the space at the venue would be closed for two years to allow for substantial renovations.
The changes, described by Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who is an ex-officio board member, and her lawyers, amount to a dramatic test of U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper. He ruled in May that letters affixed to the building that spelled out Trump’s name were added illegally and he ordered their removal, a decision that the Republican administration failed to persuade courts to overturn. At the same time, Cooper blocked a two-year closure that was set to take effect July 5, saying an earlier board vote authorizing the shuttering was “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.”
“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” Beatty said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”
A representative of the Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Much of Thursday’s board meeting was expected to focus on the extent of closures required to allow for renovations that the Kennedy Center’s management says are needed to improve safety. In response to the judge’s criticism of the earlier vote, the institution’s leaders said they would provide the board with three options to consider.
They included a complete closure or a partial closure that would allow “some continued public access and limited programming in spaces unaffected” by the work. A third option would “consider a highly limited series of phased closures to address only the Center’s most serious infrastructure needs while scheduling and maintaining a full slate of programming.”
Ultimately, the board decided to close the building for two years while leaving the potential for some degree of programming to still happen in an outdoor space known as the Reach. The decision to move ahead with the two-year closure, in addition to the moves to memorialize Trump, could revive questions about whether the board seriously considered the full range of options.
During Trump’s second term, the Kennedy Center has become an unlikely — and highly visible — metaphor of presidential power. While he largely ignored the institution during his first round in Washington, Trump moved quickly to oust the institution’s leadership when he returned to office in January 2025 and replaced it with a board of trustees that named him chairman.
His name was quickly added to the building, before coming down in June in response to Cooper’s order. The area where it once stood is now covered by a massive tarp.
Trump’s push to remake the nation’s capital
The Kennedy Center moves are part of Trump’s broader push to reshape the physical landscape of the nation’s capital in ways that have few modern parallels.
He demolished the East Wing of the White House and is building a controversial ballroom in its place, though an appeals court ruled last week that construction should stop because Congress didn’t approve the project. Trump has said he will take the case to the Supreme Court.
His remodel of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has also stumbled after algae returned and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro refuted his claims that a vandal was responsible for the damage.
Meanwhile, Trump is planning extensive renovations of a golf course in East Potomac Park, which could significantly reduce the public’s access to running and biking paths. He is also moving forward with a triumphal arch that will sit near Arlington National Cemetery.
Trump has derided the Kennedy Center as “rusted, rotted, and rat and bug infested” and threatened to hand the building over to Congress after Cooper rejected the closure and the addition of the president’s name to the building.
The institution’s leadership has argued that it’s in genuine need of repair and updating.
Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center’s executive director and chief operating officer, guided a group of journalists through the building in April, highlighting severe water damage that he said corroded steel in some places as thin as tissue paper. Some pieces of equipment, including several 800-ton chillers that help cool the building, are decades old and in need of replacement.
At the time, Floca said he considered doing the repairs individually but insisted it was his recommendation to Trump to close the building and move forward with the renovation all at once.
“When the president asked: ‘How do you make these projects the best? How do you make them really excellent and deliver them efficiently?’ my recommendation was you close the building and you do everything over a definite period of time, two years,” he said.
More recently, the legal battles became the subject of barbs and jokes as comedian Bill Maher accepted the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in late June. At the start of the program, Pamella Roland DeVos, a Kennedy Center trustee appointed by Trump, described the institution as a “national cultural center open not just for some but for every American patron who wants to experience the greatest art and expression the world has to offer.”
“The responsibility that comes with it is one our board takes very seriously,” she said.
Across the river in Arlington
A two-year shutdown would take the region’s largest performing arts venue offline at a time when Arlington stages have been doing well. Signature Theatre and Synetic Theater both broke sales records in 2025, during the first year of upheaval at the Kennedy Center, though leaders of both companies told ARLnow at the time that it was difficult to trace a direct connection.
Signature, at 4200 Campbell Avenue, led all D.C.-area theaters in Helen Hayes Award nominations earlier this year and in May announced a 37th season built around two Sondheim productions and its first co-production with Shakespeare Theatre Company.
Other Arlington groups have a more direct stake in the building itself. The Arlington-based National Chamber Ensemble played a sold-out Kennedy Center concert in June 2025 — a performance of Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons” with guest host Lynda Carter that Artistic Director Leo Sushansky said filled the house despite boycotts of the venue. A two-year closure would take that stage off the table.
The turmoil has also surfaced in local politics. During this summer’s Democratic County Board primary, candidate James DeVita campaigned on building an Arlington arts center — an idea he said stemmed from Trump’s takeover of the Kennedy Center — and drew skepticism from his opponents over the $60-80 million price tag.
Trump’s other project on this side of the river, the 250-foot arch proposed for Memorial Circle, is still moving through federal review. Arlington planning staff raised traffic and pedestrian safety concerns about it last month, and Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) — whose parents, grandparents and sister are buried at Arlington National Cemetery — introduced a bill to block the arch in May that would bar the structure outright and permanently prohibit federal funds from being spent on one.

The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to add President Donald Trump's name to the building's facade, according to US Congresswoman Joyce Beatty.
The board also voted to proceed with a two-year closure of the performing arts venue in the US capital, Washington, D.C., for major renovations.
The decision comes after a federal judge in May ordered Trump's name to be removed from the building, ruling that only Congress can change the institution's name or authorize major alterations.
"This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court's ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed," Beatty, a Democrat who is also an ex-officio board member, said in a statement. "I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument."
The latest vote revives a dispute that has been unfolding since Trump reshaped the center's leadership after returning to office.
Why was Trump's name on the building in the first place?
Trump became interested in the Kennedy Center's operations after winning the 2024 election. He installed a mostly handpicked board that named him chairman, and his name was added to the building's facade in December.
The move was part of a broader effort to overhaul the institution. At the time, the president also announced a two-year closure of the performing arts venue for renovations that were scheduled to begin in July.
That decision soon faced a legal challenge. In May, Judge Christopher Cooper said, "the Kennedy Center's organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board's unilateral say-so."
The Kennedy Center dispute became one of several obstacles to Trump's broader efforts to remake prominent Washington landmarks. An appeals court last week halted his planned White House ballroom after he demolished the East Wing.
His Reflecting Pool renovation also faced major problems, though he still plans to build a massive Memorial Arch.
How has the Kennedy Center board justified the move?
"In its meeting today, the board voted to change the front of the building's facade to read 'The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump,' and renamed the physical site 'the President Donald J. Trump Plaza,'" Congresswoman Beatty said.
According to The New York Times, an inscription underneath the institution's name would read: "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

The Kennedy Center’s board of directors voted Thursday to place President Donald Trump’s name on the performing arts complex in recognition of his administration’s planned renovation of the historic Washington venue, opening another chapter in an ongoing legal and political fight over changes to the center.
Under the resolution approved by the board, an inscription beneath the building’s primary signage would state: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump,” sources told The New York Times.

The latest resolution is separate from an earlier board decision involving Trump’s name.
Last year, the Kennedy Center board voted to add Trump’s name to the facility, a move that triggered substantial criticism and was followed by the departure of some longtime organizations and participants associated with the center.
Among those leaving was the Washington National Opera, one of the venue’s prominent institutional fixtures.
Thursday’s action instead links Trump’s name specifically to the proposed restoration and renovation project through language crediting him for the work.
The renovation itself has also become the subject of controversy because of the administration’s effort to temporarily close the Kennedy Center while construction proceeds.

The new inscription vote therefore arrives while both the physical renovation strategy and attempts to place Trump’s name on the building remain entangled in litigation.

The Kennedy Center remains one of the nation’s most prominent performing arts institutions and serves as a national memorial to President John F. Kennedy.
The board’s decision does not by itself resolve the outstanding legal questions surrounding the inscription or the broader renovation plans.
Instead, Thursday’s vote establishes the board’s preferred wording — “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” — while the courts continue to determine how far the administration and the center’s leadership may go in altering the building and its operations.

Kennedy Center Board Risks Court Contempt After Voting To Add Trump Name To Building Despite Ruling
Board's decision to credit Trump for renovations could defy court ruling
The Kennedy Center board has voted to put President Donald Trump's name back on the Washington arts institution despite a federal court ruling that said his name could not legally be added without congressional action.
The move places the Trump-led board in a fresh confrontation with the judiciary and could force U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper to decide whether the latest action complies with his earlier orders.
The board voted Thursday to proceed with a two-year closure of the Kennedy Center's main building for a roughly $250 million renovation and separately approved adding an inscription beneath the institution's main signage reading, 'Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.' Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex officio member of the board who has challenged the renaming in court, condemned the decision as an attempt to circumvent the court.
The controversy matters because the board is not simply revisiting a political naming dispute. In May, Cooper ruled that Congress — not the Kennedy Center board — has the authority to change the name of the federally established memorial to John F. Kennedy. Trump's name was subsequently removed from the building in June after the courts declined to pause the order while the case was appealed. A federal appeals court reaffirmed in July that the name had to remain off the building during the appeal.
Why a $250M Renovation May Be Trump's Back Door to the Kennedy Center
The latest vote does not formally rename the Kennedy Center in the same way as the board's December 2025 action. Instead, the board approved an inscription crediting Trump for the planned restoration.
That distinction could become central to the next stage of the legal battle. The wording approved by the board would be placed beneath the Kennedy Center's principal signage and would prominently associate Trump's name with the federally designated institution.
Beatty said the decision was a 'transparent effort to circumvent the Court's ruling' and argued that it conflicts with the laws establishing the Kennedy Center as a memorial to Kennedy. She has indicated that she intends to challenge the board's latest action.
The legal risk is particularly significant because the courts have already rejected an attempt to restore Trump's name during the appeal. On July 8, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit denied the board's request for a stay. The panel noted that the Kennedy Center had complied with Cooper's May order by removing Trump's name from the façade and related materials.
That does not automatically mean Thursday's vote amounts to contempt of court. Cooper must now determine what legal effect the new resolution has and whether the board has complied with the specific requirements of his existing orders. The Kennedy Center is required to submit details of its latest plans to the judge for review.
The $250 Million Renovation Is Also Back in Court
Cooper previously blocked the board's plan to close the institution for two years, finding that trustees had failed to properly consider the centre's statutory responsibilities and the consequences of shutting down programming. He described the earlier closure decision as 'ill-informed and seemingly preordained'.
The board has now voted again to pursue a major renovation. The proposal includes structural repairs, new marble flooring, acoustic improvements and interior upgrades. The Kennedy Center's newer Reach facility would remain open for limited programming while the main building is closed. The project is expected to keep the principal building out of operation until 2028.
This time, however, the board has undertaken what it says is more extensive deliberation following Cooper's criticism.
Trump Forces Builders To Rip up New White House Helipad After Frantic Around-The-Clock Shifts
The dispute began in December 2025, when Trump's newly reconstituted board voted to add his name to the institution. Crews quickly placed his name on the building, turning the Kennedy Center into one of the most visible symbols of Trump's efforts to reshape Washington's cultural institutions.
Cooper's May ruling then established a crucial legal boundary: the Kennedy Center's statutory name could not be changed unilaterally by its board. The appeals court's July decision left that ruling in force while the broader appeal continues.
For now, the Trump name remains legally contested rather than officially restored. The immediate question is whether Cooper will accept the board's new approach as a lawful renovation inscription — or view it as an attempt to achieve indirectly what the court has already prohibited directly.

The Kennedy Centre board voted on Thursday to add US President Donald Trump’s name to the facade of the performing arts venue and move forward with a two-year closure, according to congresswoman Joyce Beatty, a trustee through her position in Congress, and her lawyers.
A representative for the Kennedy Centre did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The moves set up a test of US District Judge Christopher Cooper, who ruled in May that letters affixed to the building and spelling out Trump’s name were added illegally.
The judge ordered them removed and at the same time blocked a closure that was set to take effect on July 5, saying that an earlier board vote endorsing the move was “ill-informed and seemingly preordained”.
“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the court’s ruling and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio who is an ex officio board member, said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”
During Trump’s second term, the Kennedy Centre has become an unlikely – and highly visible – metaphor of presidential power.

sources.text:
The board of the John F. Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts voted today to add an inscription bearing President Donald Trump's name to the building's exterior, according to Democratic U.S. Representative Joyce Beatty, a move that could set up a clash with a federal judge who previously ordered his name removed from the facade.
"In its meeting today, the board voted to change the front of the building's facade to read 'The John F. Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump,' and renamed the physical site 'the President Donald J. Trump Plaza,'" said Ms Beatty, an ex officio member on the center's board.
A second source with knowledge of the situation confirmed the decision.
The New York Times, citing a resolution, reported earlier today "that the centre desires to recognize and honor President Trump's existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the center by all legal means."
The board - dominated by Trump loyalists - also voted to close the Kennedy Centre for two years, according to Ms Beatty, who sued the Trump administration and the centre over what she called an unlawful name change and the planned closure.
The Trump administration in December added Mr Trump's name to the facade of the Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts.
But in May a judge ordered the removal of Trump's name, ruling that the iconic Washington venue cannot be renamed without an act of Congress.
A federal appeals court last month denied the administration's bid to keep Trump's name on the building while it pursues court action to restore it.
Workers stripped Trump's name from the Kennedy Center in June.
The Trump administration argued that removing Trump's name would hurt fundraising and worsen the center's finances.
The appeals court said those claims were not supported by specific facts or evidence.

sources.news_title: Defying Federal Judge, Kennedy Center Board Votes to Close, Inscribe Trump’s Name on Building
sources.text:
The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to close the center for renovations for a second time, while keeping a smaller, separate theater open.
This week’s vote marked a dramatic escalation in the legal battle over the historic center: the Trump-allied board also moved to inscribe the president’s name beneath the signage—a direct rebuke of a May federal court order that had blocked both the closure and a name change. According to the New York Times, the board has approved an inscription beneath the center’s name reading: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”
The Kennedy Center board voted last December to change the institution’s name to include Trump and to add his name to the marble facade, triggering a financial crisis as performers began dropping from the roster in protest. In the ensuing months, the White House, federal courts, and Washington preservationists have been locked in a legal standoff over where the authority to rename the center lies. Legal experts noted the name change may violate a stipulation established after Congress renamed the center following John F. Kennedy’s assassination in 1963.
US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled on May 29 that the board had acted unlawfully in renaming the institution, finding that only Congress held that power. He also found the board had acted unlawfully in approving a two-year closure for renovations.
Until now, the Trump administration had pursued conventional legal channels to fight the ruling: first a motion in June, which was denied. The President’s name was removed from the facade that month, and scrubbed from the center’s letterhead, website, and other official branding. In July, a federal appeals court denied a bid to restore Trump’s name, finding that the administration had failed to prove the arts complex would be “irreparably injured” by the institution reverting to its original name.
The board’s Thursday resolution reportedly directed officials to pursue “all legal means” to defend what it called President Trump‘s rescue of the center “from the brink of disaster.”
“It is hereby resolved, that the center desires to recognize and honor President Trump’s existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the center by all legal means,” the measure said, according to the Times. The meeting was held virtually and not open to the public.
The Kennedy Center, whose chairman has been Trump since February 2025, voted this past March to close the institution for two years for renovations. Judge Cooper blocked the closure, calling it “derelict” for the board to vote without considering the impact on the capital’s leading performing arts institution.
“The board will be expected to prepare itself with sufficient information to make a considered, independent decision,” the judge wrote in May, “taking account of its obligation to both maintain and operate a premiere arts venue and its solemn duty to memorialize a fallen president.”
In response, the president took to social media to berate Judge Cooper as an “anti-Trump hater” and predict that the center would “soon be closed, probably never to open again.” Throughout the case, the institution has argued that removing then restoring the president’s name would waste “time and money” and risk losing donor gifts given only “with the name ‘Trump’ on the building.”
Judge Cooper is expected to soon review—again—the legality of the latest closure and renaming decisions.
The Kennedy Center has grown increasingly marooned from its many patrons and performing arts peers in recent months, and today has a starkly sparse programming schedule. In January, celebrated composer Philip Glass announced his withdrawal of a symphony honoring Abraham Lincoln that was scheduled for its first-ever performance by the National Symphony Orchestra in June. Meanwhile, the Washington National Opera, which had performed there since 1971, moved out in January, citing low attendance.
ARTnews has contacted the Kennedy Center for comment.

Kennedy Center board votes to partially close arts center during renovations and add Trump’s name to the building again
sources.text:
The Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board voted Thursday to partially close the iconic arts center for up to two years during renovations and to re-add President Donald Trump’s name to the building’s facade, according to a person who attended the virtual board meeting and a second person familiar with the meeting.
The decision would close the Kennedy Center’s main building and keep a smaller addition, known as the Reach, open for some events in response to a May court order requiring the board to maintain the center as a memorial to President John F. Kennedy.
After an almost two-hour Zoom meeting, the board voted 20-3 to change the name of the building to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” and the physical location to “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick proposed the name change.
Trump, who appointed himself chairman of the board last year, joined the call for several minutes, according to the source who attended the meeting.
The three people voting against it are the ex officio members from Congress, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio; Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; and Rep. Rick Larsen, D-Wash.
“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” Beatty, who was one of the plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the Kennedy Center’s renaming, said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”
Attorneys for Beatty said in a statement that the new naming effort appears to defy a judge’s ruling this year that the center’s board does not have the authority to rename what was intended as a “living memorial” for an assassinated president.
“A federal judge already rejected the board’s unlawful attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, and told Donald Trump’s handpicked board that its last closure vote was ill-informed and preordained. Today’s vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts,” said the lawyers, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group.
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper’s order in May, which temporarily blocked the Kennedy Center’s planned closure last month, also asked that the board provide a financial plan to justify the decision to close it. Keeping the smaller venue open would allow ticket sales for some events, including performances by the National Symphony Orchestra, which is the Kennedy Center’s chief tenant.
The orchestra has performed there since the early 1970s, when the center — conceived by Jaqueline Kennedy as a memorial to her slain husband — opened.
In recent years, under the baton of music director and principal conductor Giancarlo Noseda, it has been rising in stature — but its future is now uncertain because the Kennedy Center’s Concert Hall will not be available. A search for other venues in the area has been underway.
The Kennedy Center’s future has been in limbo for months as Trump moves to reshape the iconic art institution in his image, one of several major Washington renovation projects.
After Trump named himself the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year and filled its board with allies, the board voted unanimously in March to close the center for two years for renovations.
Cooper’s order temporarily blocked the construction work and ordered that Trump’s name be removed, which it was in June.
He also said the board could still ultimately close the center “should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion.”
Cooper also found the board did not have the authority to rename the center or add a name to it without the approval of Congress, which initially named it.
“The Kennedy Center’s organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board’s unilateral say-so,” Cooper said in his May decision.
“May the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts be renamed absent Congressional authorization? The answer, plain from the face of the statute, is no. Nor can any other individual be memorialized on the front portico of the building. Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it.”
The decision to close the center and add Trump’s name to the building has sparked outrage from the administration’s critics, as well as members of the Kennedy family.
Former Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, a grandnephew of the late president, said in a statement last year that the center “is a living memorial to a fallen president and named for President Kennedy by federal law. It can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.”
