WASHINGTON — The Kennedy Center board voted on Thursday to add President Donald Trump's name to the facade of the performing arts venue and move forward with a two-year closure, according to Rep. Joyce Beatty, a trustee through her position in Congress, and her lawyers.
A representative for the Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The moves set up a test of U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who ruled in May that letters affixed to the building and spelling out Trump's name were added illegally. The judge ordered them removed and at the same time blocked a closure that was set to take effect July 5, saying that an earlier board vote endorsing the move was "ill-informed and seemingly preordained."
"This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court's ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed," Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio who is an ex officio board member, said in a statement. "I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument."
During Trump's second term, the Kennedy Center has become an unlikely — and highly visible — metaphor of presidential power. While he largely ignored the institution during his first round in Washington, Trump moved quickly to oust the institution's leadership when he returned to office in January 2025 and replaced it with a board of trustees that named him chairman. His name was quickly added to the building, a move that Cooper also declared illegal.
The Republican's name came down from the building in June but the area where it once stood is now covered by a massive tarp.
The Kennedy Center moves are part of Trump's broader push to reshape the physical landscape of the nation's capital in ways that have few modern parallels.
He demolished the East Wing of the White House and is building a controversial ballroom in its place, though an appeals court ruled last week that construction should stop because Congress didn't approve the project. Trump has said he will take the case to the Supreme Court.
His remodel of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has also stumbled after algae returned and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro refuted his claims that a vandal was responsible for the damage.
Meanwhile, Trump is planning extensive renovations of a golf course in East Potomac Park, which could significantly reduce the public's access to running and biking paths. He is also moving forward with a triumphal arch that will sit near Arlington National Cemetery.
Trump has derided the Kennedy Center as "rusted, rotted, and rat and bug infested" and threatened to hand the building over to Congress after Cooper rejected the closure and the addition of the president's name to the building.
The institution's leadership has argued that it's in genuine need of repair and updating.
Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's executive director and chief operating officer, guided a group of journalists through the building in April, highlighting severe water damage that he said corroded steel in some places as thin as tissue paper. Some pieces of equipment, including several 800-ton chillers that help cool the building, are decades old and in need of replacement.
At the time, Floca said he considered doing the repairs individually but insisted it was his recommendation to Trump to close the building and move forward with the renovation all at once.
"When the president asked: 'How do you make these projects the best? How do you make them really excellent and deliver them efficiently?' my recommendation was you close the building and you do everything over a definite period of time, two years," he said.
More recently, the legal battles became the subject of barbs and jokes as comedian Bill Maher accepted the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in late June. At the start of the program, Pamella Roland DeVos, a Kennedy Center trustee appointed by Trump, described the institution as a "national cultural center open not just for some but for every American patron who wants to experience the greatest art and expression the world has to offer."
"The responsibility that comes with it is one our board takes very seriously," she said.

sources.text:
As the Iran war looks to have no end, gas prices rise again, and court cases keep turning against him, Trump is desperate for a new distraction. Too many of his currently active ones have fallen apart and the MAGA faithful might actually begin to notice reality. So, to provide the new distraction (and feed his endless ego) it seems that the Donald has once again turned his sights on the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
The New York Times is reporting that the Kennedy Center Board has taken two votes that are looking to get around Judge Christopher Cooper’s order that Trump’s name be removed and that the Board justify any closure to him. While it’s possible that the plan they voted on for renovations may (or may not) pass muster with the Judge, it still looks like it’s meant to primarily serve the distraction and ego-fluffing goals far more than anything else.
The board voted on Thursday to close the Kennedy Center’s main building, while keeping a newer addition to the campus, known as the Reach, open for limited programming and to operate as an active memorial to John F. Kennedy.
Ahead of the meeting, the board was presented with a 163-page plan for a $250 million “renewal” project that includes structural repair work, new marble floors, $11.8 million in “acoustical improvements” and a plan to temporarily move the famous 3,000-pound bronze bust of Kennedy to another building on campus.
This plan would keep the main building closed until the summer of 2028. It sounds an awful lot like Trump’s original “renovation” plans, that is putting his same tacky stamp on it, which is very much the distraction part. The whole thing is a “look over there and pay no attention to the disasters and scandals behind the curtain.”
But then we get to the more open defiance of Judge Cooper. The other vote they took today was to add an inscription to the stone on the front of the building, under it’s name: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.” This is one of the most juvenile work-arounds I’ve seen in a while, and I teach high school students. This is both a fantastic distraction and a blatant sop to Trump’s ego after the Judge made them take his name off after the first try at this.
So there we have it. Our dementia-addled despot has his flunkies on the Kennedy Center Board provide the distraction he needs and the ego-boost he craves all in one stupid assault on another beloved institution. It will be a great day indeed in America when we no longer have to worry about what stupid thing our president might do today to try to cover for their failures. But we can all do our best to see that future into being, starting in November.

The Kennedy Center Board of Trustees on Thursday voted to move forward with President Trump’s plan to close the building for renovations for two years, according to the Associated Press. During the same meeting, the board, which is filled with the president’s allies, also voted to inscribe Trump’s name on the building.
The votes came after a federal judge in May ordered a halt to Trump’s plan to close the center, and also that Trump’s name be removed from the building, where it had been added to the venue’s official name. The board’s recent vote came after it reviewed information about the repercussions and costs of a closure. This included three scenarios: a full closure, a partial closure over a period of five years and a limited series of phased closures, sources close to the situation told the AP, asking to remain anonymous.
President Trump says he will move to close the Kennedy Center performing arts venue for two years starting in July for construction.
It is unclear if the recent vote will again face legal pushback.
The Kennedy Center has been in crisis for more than a year, beginning in February 2025 when Trump fired its board and appointed himself chairman. He swiftly selected Richard Grenell, a former ambassador to Germany and a staunch ally, as acting director of the center. Under Trump and Grenell, the venue ruptured audiences and lost a slew of high-profile shows and artists including “Hamilton,” Shonda Rhimes and Ben Folds. The Washington National Opera also left the venue, which it had occupied for decades.
The situation worsened late last year after the board voted to rename the venue the Donald J. Trump and the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts. Performers, including jazz musician Chuck Redd, canceled a variety of holiday shows. The Kennedy Center threatened to sue Redd, creating a legal drama that continued until this week when a superior court judge in Washington, D.C., ordered the center to pay more than $250,000 to Redd to cover attorneys’ fees and other legal costs.

sources.news_title: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Carve Trump’s Name Into the Building’s Marble Facade
sources.text:
The Kennedy Center’s board voted Thursday to inscribe President Donald Trump’s name into the storied building’s white marble facade and proceed with a lengthy shutdown of the venue to accommodate an extensive $250 million renovation project, according to ex officio member Rep. Joyce Beatty.
The decision comes just months after a judge ruled that separate signage bearing the president’s name had to be taken off the building’s marquee. The new inscription will test the order, though due to ongoing litigation the judge has the power to delay the projects.
The board, which Trump fired en masse last year and restocked with allies, voted to close the center’s main building, while The Reach, a newer expansion to the facility, will remain open for limited events. It will also serve as a memorial to former President John F. Kennedy.
The president announced the renovations in February and said the center would need to close for two years.
Trending
An outside consulting firm concluded that keeping the main building open during the construction project would be significantly more expensive. The board reviewed a 163-page plan for the $250 million renovation project ahead of the meeting, according to The New York Times.
The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The new inscription, which is set to read “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump,” will be placed under the marquee bearing President John F. Kennedy’s name, according to Beatty. The board also approved a motion to rename the physical site on which the center stands to “The President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”
Following Thursday’s meeting, Beatty lashed out at the Kennedy Center board members who green-lit the changes.
“This morning’s decision to close the Center and the surprise agenda item to put Donald Trump’s name back on the building was more of the same,” Beatty wrote in a statement. “This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed. I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”
Trump’s push to renovate the Kennedy Center — including affixing his name to the front marble exterior — has launched several monthslong court battles and prompted congressional scrutiny over funding for the renovations.
Trump’s handpicked board had initially sought to rebrand the center and place his name on top of Kennedy’s, dubbing the institution the “Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.”
But U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued an opinion in May that blocked the proposed renovation project and halted the center’s renaming in response to a lawsuit filed by Beatty.
Cooper ruled that the board had been “derelict” by neglecting the potential impact the renovation could have on the programming at the center.
Trump railed against Cooper’s decision at the time, calling him a “Highly Conflicted, Crooked Federal Judge” and saying the Kennedy Center is “broken, unsafe, and busted,” in a post on Truth Social in May.
The Trump-backed renovations at the Kennedy Center come amid a wave of beautification projects at government buildings across D.C. — including the addition of a large ballroom at White House and the refurbishment of historic landmarks like the Reflecting Pool.

Kennedy Center board votes to add Trump's name below building's sign
The board, composed mostly of hand-picked members selected by Trump, also voted to partially close the center for renovations.
WASHINGTON – The Kennedy Center's board of trustees voted to inscribe President Donald Trump's name below the sign on the iconic institution's building and once again temporarily close the bulk of the performing arts venue for renovations, testing the two key components of a federal judge's order.
The actions came during a closed-door Aug. 13 board meeting on Zoom, according to a source with direct knowledge of the votes who confirmed deliberations reported first by The New York Times.
The board, composed mostly of hand-picked members selected by Trump, approved a resolution to add the inscription “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump" directly underneath the Kennedy Center's facade sign. The same resolution directs the center to honor Trump for saving the center from the "brink of disaster," according to The Times, suggesting as another possibility the renaming of the center's grounds to "the President Donald J. Trump Plaza."
The board voted to partially close the Kennedy Center for renovations, a project Trump has previously said would take two years. The plan calls for closing the Kennedy's Center main building while keeping open a newer, significantly smaller theater wing called the REACH.
The planned inscription of Trump's name is an attempt to work around a federal judge's order in May to remove the president's name from the center's title, signage and branding. U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper, in the same order, blocked the board's March vote to close the center for two years for renovations, arguing that the action lacked serious consideration by the board.
Democratic U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, the plaintiff in a lawsuit that led to the judge's ruling, slammed the board's latest actions as "more of the same."
“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed. I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument," said Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's board, who is represented in court by the group Democracy Defenders Action.
Trump's name was added to the Kennedy Center building in December 2025 after the president's takeover of the board and renaming of the institution as the "Trump-Kennedy Center."
In his May ruling, Cooper said the board violated the 1964 federal law that created the center in honor of President John F. Kennedy, arguing that the statute makes clear "the Kennedy Center must be named for, and is meant to honor, President Kennedy alone." Congressional approval would be required to change the name from the Kennedy Center, the judge said.
The Kennedy Center on June 13 complied with the judge's directive to remove Trump's name from the building's sign, but not until hours after a court deadline passed. The center's Trump-aligned staff left up a massive tarp that prevents the public from seeing the sign without Trump's name. The tarp remains over the facade of the center.
In blocking the board's previous attempt to close the Kennedy center for renovations, Cooper said the decision was made hastily at the direction of Matt Floca, the center's executive director, without the board having an opportunity to adequately review the matter.
The Kennedy Center's legal counsel has argued that the judge did not rule against the concept of temporarily closing the center; rather, that the board's vote was "inappropriate and that any subsequent vote must take more information into account."

Trump’s Kennedy Center board votes to put his name back on the building — despite a judge’s explicit order
sources.text:
Having been ordered by a federal judge to remove President Donald Trump’s name from the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., Trump’s handpicked board has devised a new way to put it back.
The board voted Thursday to inscribe “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” beneath the building’s principal signage, The New York Times reports, citing two people with direct knowledge of the private proceedings.
The resolution directs center officials to recognize Trump through “all legal means” and suggests naming the grounds the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” It credits Trump with bringing the institution back “from the brink of disaster.”
The proposal challenges a May ruling by U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who found that the board lacked authority to rename the institution. Congress designated the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts as the nation’s living memorial to the assassinated president, and federal law generally bars additional memorials or memorial-like plaques in its public spaces.
“Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it,” Cooper wrote in his accompanying opinion.
Trump took control of the Kennedy Center in February 2025, removing trustees, installing political allies, making himself chairman and placing gay Republican operative Richard Grenell in charge. Trump said he wanted to eliminate the center’s family-friendly drag programming.
As The Advocate previously reported, the institution subsequently removed LGBTQ+ programming, including a planned WorldPride concert involving the Gay Men’s Chorus of Washington, D.C. Artists withdrew, productions relocated, audiences stayed away, and ticket sales plunged.
Trump’s board voted in December to rename the institution the “Trump Kennedy Center.” Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, an ex officio trustee whom the board had stripped of her voting rights, sued. Cooper ordered Trump’s name removed, restored voting rights to ex officio trustees and temporarily blocked the board’s plan to close the center for two years.
Workers removed Trump’s lettering overnight June 12-13, but The Advocate reported that scaffolding and tarps remained, preventing the public from seeing the restored facade. Cooper subsequently ordered the parties to explain the covering’s purpose and status. Beatty’s attorneys accused Trump’s allies of “willfully sabotaging Kennedy Center’s iconic façade” after losing in court.
The board voted Thursday again to close the main building for renovations, according to the Times. Trustees were presented with a 163-page plan for a roughly $250 million project that would include structural repairs, new marble floors, acoustical work and $7 million in restroom renovations. The newer Reach complex would remain open for limited programming and Kennedy memorial exhibits.
Cooper had described the board’s first closure decision as “ill-informed and seemingly preordained,” but allowed trustees to reconsider it after conducting proper analysis. The Kennedy Center must submit its new plan to him next week.

sources.news_title: Kennedy Center board votes to add Trump name to performing arts building
sources.text:
WASHINGTON -- The battle over the Kennedy Center’s future escalated Thursday as U.S. President Donald Trump’s allies on the board took new steps to commemorate him with physical changes to the iconic performing arts institution that could defy a federal court order.
During an hourslong meeting that was conducted virtually, the board voted to add Trump’s name to the building’s facade so it would read “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump.” The plaza in front of the building would be named after Trump and most of the space at the venue would be closed for two years to allow for substantial renovations.
The changes, described by Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who is an ex-officio board member, and her lawyers, amount to a dramatic test of U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper.
He ruled in May that letters affixed to the building that spelled out Trump’s name were added illegally and he ordered their removal, a decision that the Republican administration failed to persuade courts to overturn. At the same time, Cooper blocked a two-year closure that was set to take effect July 5, saying an earlier board vote authorizing the shuttering was “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.”
“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” Beatty said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”
A Kennedy Center representative did not respond to a request for comment.
Much of Thursday’s board meeting was expected to focus on the extent of closures required to allow for renovations that the Kennedy Center’s management says are needed to improve safety. In response to the judge’s criticism of the earlier vote, the institution’s leaders said they would provide the board with three options to consider.
They included a complete closure or a partial closure that would allow “some continued public access and limited programming in spaces unaffected” by the work. A third option would “consider a highly limited series of phased closures to address only the centre’s most serious infrastructure needs while scheduling and maintaining a full slate of programming.”
Ultimately, the board decided to close the building for two years while leaving the potential for some degree of programming to still happen in an outdoor space known as the Reach. The decision to move ahead with the two-year closure, in addition to the moves to memorialize Trump, could revive questions about whether the board seriously considered the full range of options, a point Democrats emphasized after the meeting.
Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat who is also an ex officio board member, criticized a “sham meeting.”
“What happened today was nothing more than a rubber stamp on a decision the President made months ago that the Board already tried to effectuate without doing proper due diligence,” he said in a statement.
The Kennedy Center has become a metaphor for presidential power
During Trump’s second term, the Kennedy Center has become an unlikely -- and highly visible -- metaphor for presidential power. While he largely ignored the institution during his first term in Washington, Trump moved quickly to oust its leadership when he returned to office in January 2025 and replaced it with a board of trustees that named him chairman.
His name was quickly added to the building, before coming down in June in response to Cooper’s order. The area where it once stood is now covered by a massive tarp.
The Kennedy Center moves are part of Trump’s broader push to reshape the physical landscape of the nation’s capital in ways that have few modern parallels.
He demolished the East Wing of the White House and is building a controversial ballroom in its place, though an appeals court ruled last week that construction should stop because Congress didn’t approve the project. Trump has said he will take the case to the Supreme Court.
His remodel of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has also stumbled after algae returned and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro refuted his claims that a vandal was responsible for the damage.
Meanwhile, Trump is planning extensive renovations of a golf course in East Potomac Park, which could significantly reduce the public’s access to running and biking paths. He is also moving forward with a triumphal arch that will sit near Arlington National Cemetery.
Trump has derided the Kennedy Center as “rusted, rotted, and rat and bug infested” and threatened to hand the building over to Congress after Cooper rejected the closure and the addition of the president’s name to the building.
The institution’s leadership has argued that it’s in genuine need of repair and updating.
Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center’s executive director and chief operating officer, guided a group of journalists through the building in April, highlighting severe water damage that he said corroded steel in some places as thin as tissue paper. Some pieces of equipment, including several 800-ton chillers that help cool the building, are decades old and in need of replacement.
At the time, Floca said he considered doing the repairs individually but insisted it was his recommendation to Trump to close the building and move forward with the renovation all at once.
“When the president asked, `How do you make these projects the best? How do you make them really excellent and deliver them efficiently?’ My recommendation was you close the building and you do everything over a definite period of time, two years,” he said.
More recently, the legal battles became the subject of barbs and jokes as comedian Bill Maher accepted the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in late June. At the start of the program, Pamella Roland DeVos, a Kennedy Center trustee appointed by Trump, described the institution as a “national cultural centre open not just for some but for every American patron who wants to experience the greatest art and expression the world has to offer.”
“The responsibility that comes with it is one our board takes very seriously,” she said.

sources.text:
Kennedy Center finds questionable workaround to etch Trump’s name on the building — again
Trump-controlled board agrees to add the president’s name to the venue, directly below the sign
Donald Trump’s administration has insisted for months that the Kennedy Center stands to lose millions of dollars without his name on the building after losing several legal battles to rename the venue after himself.
On Thursday, the performing arts institution’s Trump-controlled board of trustees agreed to do just that.
The board voted, again, to close the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts for renovations as part of a plan announced by the president earlier this year, which was blocked by a federal judge and is tied up in ongoing litigation. That plan included putting Trump’s name on the white marble facade, in front of the name of the assassinated former president, by renaming the venue The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts.
But under the resolution approved by the board Thursday, Trump’s name will appear on the building to thank the president for the multi-million dollar renovations. An inscription will read “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” — directly below the sign.
“This morning’s decision to close the Center and the surprise agenda item to put Donald Trump’s name back on the building was more of the same,” said Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, who is suing to stop the building’s closure and Trump-led renovations. “This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed.”
After Trump announced the building’s two-year closure this year, a board largely composed of his allies agreed — and construction crews got to work installing his name in heavy metal letters to the front of the building.
Beatty sued, arguing that the Trump-led rebranding illegally circumvented Congress and that the board’s approval was “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.”
In May, Washington, D.C., District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that Congress made it “crystal clear” that the building is only to be named after Kennedy, “and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial” based on a “unilateral say-so.”
The latest move to add Trump’s name to the building appears to be a legally dubious workaround. Federal law invoked by Beatty and Cooper states that “no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas.”
The Kennedy Center had until June 12 to strip the president’s name from the building following Coper’s order, but construction crews in hard hats and neon green high-vis vests only started to assemble scaffolding to reach the letters that afternoon. Trump’s name plates appeared to have been removed in the dead of night in the early morning hours of June 13.
But the scaffolding and tarp are still in place, covering up where the president’s name used to be. Judge Cooper has pressed the Trump administration to find out why.
In court filings, the Department of Justice claimed the venue stands to lose “hundreds of millions” of dollars without Trump’s name attached to the building, which lawyers for the government argued should be renamed in the president’s honor after he “donated his time, energy and unparalleled Construction talents” to its renovation.
The Justice Department is appealing Cooper’s court order requiring the venue to remove Trump’s name. Without it, the venerable arts institution will fall in to “financial ruin,” according to government lawyers.
Before Thursday’s meeting, the board was presented with a 163-page proposal for renovations, which could exceed $560 million — more than double the $257 million Congress had already eyed for the project.
The resolution that was ultimately approved by Trump’s hand-picked board will approve a renovation plan from real estate firm JLL that is expected to cost roughly $250 million.
Renovations are expected to be completed by summer 2028.
According to the resolution, the board will remain “fully committed” to continue supporting arts programming during the two-year closure to maintain the “historic and architecturally significant nature of the center’s main building.”
“A federal judge already rejected the board’s unlawful attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, and told Donald Trump’ handpicked board that its last closure vote was ill-informed and preordained,” according to a statement from Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group, who are representing Beatty.
“Today’s vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts,” they added. “The court already ruled against the board when it bowed to Trump’s demands. Now, the defendants must answer for their actions — again — in court.”

The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted on Thursday to inscribe President Trump’s name on the building’s facade, as reported by The New York Times. The move would put the board in direct conflict with a federal court order requiring his name to be removed.

Critics say the monthslong Reflecting Pool saga and other demands by Trump risk undermining the integrity of a federal agency that’s long been held in high esteem by the American public.
“Never — not once in decades — have I witnessed such systematic degradation, disrespect and dismantling of the National Park Service as I see today under the thumb of President Donald Trump and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum,” said Bill Wade, a former park ranger and superintendent.
Rubio and Bessent stayed on decoy flight from Turkey as Trump switched planes, official says
The two most senior members of Trump’s Cabinet, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, flew out of last month’s NATO summit in Turkey on what was effectively a decoy plane following an Iranian threat, while Trump was secretly moved to a smaller military jet, a senior U.S. official said Wednesday.
The official, who was briefed on the situation and spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details of presidential travel, said Rubio was aware of the switch and details of the threat behind it but could or would not say why he had stayed on the plane. The official said Bessent was likely aware but did not know for sure.
The official, however, noted that security precautions for the president — especially one who has been the target of several assassination attempts — are more robust than those for even top members of the Cabinet.
Under the U.S. Constitution, the secretaries of State and Treasury follow the vice president and the highest ranking member of each chamber of Congress in the presidential line of succession.
— Matthew Lee
Kennedy Center board set to vote on whether to move forward with closure
The Kennedy Center’s board is expected to meet Thursday to consider plans for the performing arts venue’s future after a federal judge blocked an earlier move for a two-year closure that would allow for substantial renovations.
Ahead of the meeting, the Kennedy Center’s management said it would present the board with three approaches for consideration.
The options would include a complete closure or a partial closure that would allow “some continued public access and limited programming in spaces unaffected” by the work. A third option would “consider a highly limited series of phased closures to address only the Center’s most serious infrastructure needs while scheduling and maintaining a full slate of programming.”
In blocking earlier plans for closure, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled the board’s March 16 vote backing the move appeared “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” In moving forward, the board, which is largely made up of President Donald Trump’s allies, may face pressure to prove they’ve thoroughly considered their options.
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is leaving the Trump administration
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person to hold the role, will leave the Trump administration at the end of the month to spend more time with her young family.
Leavitt, 28, called it a “bittersweet decision” in a social media post Wednesday shortly after President Donald Trump announced she would be stepping down. She recently returned to the White House podium after the birth of her second child, a daughter named Viviana, in May. She also has a 2-year-old son.
“The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life,” Leavitt wrote.
Trump did not outline plans for who might replace her in the high-profile role.
